Consult Summary:
- Adult male with 4 days of viral-type upper respiratory symptoms (initial painful sore throat, nasal congestion, subsequent dry cough, night sweats, myalgias and fatigue) assessed as likely viral URTI or early influenza; advised supportive care and safety-netting.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Four days of feeling "under the weather" with sore throat, runny nose/congestion, progressing to a dry cough and generalized tiredness.
- Timeline/progression:
  - Day 0–2: Onset with sore throat and runny nose; sore throat painful with difficulty/pain on swallowing for 1–2 days, then improving.
  - Days 3–4: Increasing nasal congestion, new onset dry cough starting ~yesterday, intermittent generalized headache, new myalgias and weakness over past couple days, night sweats for ~3–4 days.
  - Initial fever at onset; fever has been decreasing with paracetamol and ibuprofen.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Symptoms improved partially with paracetamol and ibuprofen (fever control).
  - Rest and fluids recommended; patient plans to take 1–2 days off work.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - ENT: sore throat (improving), painful swallowing early on; no observed white spots or redness reported (no throat self-exam performed).
  - Nose: runny nose, progressing to congestion and nasal obstruction.
  - Cough: dry, constant, started yesterday, not particularly painful.
  - Respiratory: mild exertional breathlessness ("winded" on exertion only); no shortness of breath at rest; no chest pain.
  - Constitutional: initial fever (now settling), night sweats, fatigue, decreased appetite, increased fluid intake, intermittent generalized headaches, myalgias.
  - ENT/ears: no ear pain, no ear discharge.
  - Eyes: no visual changes, no photophobia.
  - GI/GU: no nausea, no vomiting; bowels and urine reported as normal.
  - Skin/MSK: no rash; muscle aches and joint aches present.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No chest pain at rest, no significant dyspnea at rest, no ear problems, no rash, no vomiting, no photophobia, no vision changes.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions reported; patient states he is "otherwise fit and well."
- Medications:
  - Paracetamol — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Ibuprofen — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies:
  - None reported.

Social History:
- Lives alone.
- Occupation: accountant; currently working but symptomatic and planning to take a couple days off; reports increased work stress around year-end but no mood disorder reported.
- Tobacco: occasional smoking (cigars) at company parties; not a regular smoker.
- Alcohol: conflict in transcript — initially says "No," later states "occasionally" socially; overall describes infrequent/social alcohol use.
- Recreational drug use: none reported.
- No other financial or lifestyle factors disclosed beyond work stress.

Family History:
- Grandmother with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Great-grandfather with eczema.
- No other family history of note reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: none documented.
- Examination findings: none documented.

Investigations:
- No laboratory tests, imaging, or other investigations were performed or documented.
- No COVID or influenza testing documented.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection vs early influenza
  - Assessment:
    - Four days of typical viral prodrome: sore throat (now improving), rhinorrhea/congestion, dry cough, myalgias, intermittent fever that has settled with antipyretics; clinician impression: likely viral URTI or early influenza.
  - Plan:
    - Supportive care: rest, increased oral fluids/hydration.
    - Continue symptomatic treatment with paracetamol and ibuprofen (patient already taking these) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Advise taking 1–2 days off work for recovery if possible.
    - Safety-netting: return for review if not improved within one week.
    - Urgent red flags: seek earlier medical review if high fever recurs or if breathing becomes more labored, or if chest pain develops.
    - Provide telephone contact/arrangements to return sooner if symptoms worsen.
- Issue 2: Exertional shortness of breath (mild; only on exertion)
  - Assessment:
    - Patient reports being "winded" on exertion but normal at rest; likely part of acute illness-related reduced exercise tolerance.
  - Plan:
    - Monitor symptoms; rest and avoid strenuous exercise until improved.
    - Return earlier for reassessment if dyspnea at rest, worsening exertional dyspnea, or associated chest pain occurs.
- Issue 3: Symptomatic headaches, myalgias, night sweats and decreased appetite
  - Assessment:
    - Likely systemic manifestations of acute viral illness.
  - Plan:
    - Symptomatic management with OTC analgesics (paracetamol/ibuprofen) as tolerated.
    - Rest and hydration; monitor symptom trajectory and seek review if persistent or worsening.

General plan items:
- No investigations ordered at this visit.
- Follow-up: review if symptoms persist beyond 1 week or sooner if red-flag symptoms (high fever, worsening shortness of breath, chest pain).
- Patient education provided regarding expected course (viral illnesses typically ~7 days) and warning signs prompting earlier review.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation) are not documented.
  - Physical exam findings (oropharynx inspection, chest auscultation) are not documented.
  - Medication doses, routes, and frequencies for paracetamol and ibuprofen are not documented.
  - Immunization status (influenza and COVID vaccination) not documented.
  - No diagnostic testing documented (e.g., COVID, influenza, throat swab, chest x-ray, pulse oximetry) that might be expected if clinical concern existed.
  - Smoking quantity/frequency not fully quantified.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Alcohol use: patient initially answered "No" then subsequently said "occasionally" — conflict noted.
- Transcript quality comment:
  - Transcript intelligible and adequate for clinical documentation; occasional brief pauses and overlapping speech but no major inaudible segments.
